query: Starting from a multi-element automotive alloy catalyst containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios, what single intervention could overcome activity loss and durability limitations while maintaining low platinum-group-metal consumption during transient and low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust operation, including exposure to H2O and NO and degradation associated with thermal aging or increasing mileage? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the untreated starting catalyst, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, low‐temperature ammonia (or plasma-assisted nitridation) treatment applied post‐synthesis will dope the surface of the nearly equiatomic multi‐element automotive alloy catalyst with nitrogen. This intervention will induce formation of multiple metal–nitrogen bonds and drive a surface reorganization that creates a self-passivating Pt-rich skin. In doing so, the catalyst will resist activity loss and degradation (caused by H2O/NO exposure, thermal aging, and mileage‐induced changes) while still operating with minimal platinum-group-metal usage.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-element automotive alloy catalyst comprised of nearly equiatomic ratios of platinum-group and transition metals (e.g., similar to an HEA nanoparticle catalyst on a carbon or ceramic support) used in exhaust treatment.
generation.intervention: A single-step, controlled low-temperature ammonia gas (or plasma-assisted nitridation) treatment applied post-synthesis.
generation.conditions: Testing under simulated transient exhaust conditions typical of low-temperature gasoline or hybrid-vehicle operations—with intermittent exposures to H2O and NO—and subjected to repeated thermal cycling (mimicking thermal aging and mileage accumulation).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of robust multiple metal–nitrogen bonds and the consequent in situ reorganization to form a thin Pt-enriched surface layer.
generation.mechanism: Nitrogen incorporation at the surface alters the local electronic structure via formation of metal–nitrogen bonds, which lowers the dissolution tendency of both platinum and non-platinum components. This restructured surface reduces corrosion/sintering under corrosive exhaust atmospheres, stabilizes the active sites against water and NO-induced degradation, and thereby preserves catalytic activity with minimal PGM usage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated catalyst, the nitrided catalyst will display significantly lower activity loss over extended transient operation, reduced platinum dissolution, and improved stability under thermal aging—all achieved without increasing the overall consumption of platinum-group metals.
generation.baseline: The untreated multi-element automotive alloy catalyst evaluated under the same simulated exhaust conditions.
generation.boundary: The benefit is expected most prominently under the specified low-temperature/transient automotive exhaust conditions and moderate thermal aging cycles. Effects outside these regimes (e.g., extremely high temperatures) remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends findings from N–Pt/HEA/C studies (see PMC10859931, dft_analysis and related sections showing that nitrogen doping creates beneficial metal–N bonds) and from studies on reversible structural changes in HEA clusters under NO/H2 exposure (PMC10466320, reversible_structural_change_of_hea_sub_). However, it is uncertain how directly these mechanisms translate to the complex, transient automotive exhaust environment with simultaneous H2O and NO exposure and long-term mileage-related degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst batches from identical multi-element alloy synthesis. Subject one batch to the controlled low-temperature ammonia treatment while keeping the other batch untreated. Operate both samples in a flow reactor that simulates automotive exhaust conditions—featuring transient low-temperature cycles, controlled pulses of H2O and NO, and repeated thermal cycling to mimic aging. Characterize them periodically using catalytic performance tests, structural analyses (e.g., TEM and XPS for evidence of Pt-rich skin and metal–N bonds), and Pt dissolution measurements (via ICP-MS).
measurements: Catalytic conversion efficiency and kinetic performance under simulated exhaust conditions
Retention of mass activity after defined cycling/aging tests
Surface composition and bonding (via TEM, XPS, and possibly in situ synchrotron studies)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ammonia-treated catalyst does not show at least a ~30% improvement (i.e., lower activity loss and reduced Pt dissolution) compared to the untreated catalyst under identical testing conditions, or if detailed structural analysis fails to reveal the intended formation of a Pt-rich surface with significant metal–N bonding, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Interestingly, the CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NR specimen exhibited different regeneration properties from those for monometallic Pd/CeO2-NRs (Figure 7d–f). The initially flat XANES spectrum transitioned to a shape typical of monometallic Pd upon the introduction of NO. In the case of the FT-EXAFS spectra, the peak attributed to short Pd–M bonds at approximately 2.1 Å disappeared and a peak related to long Pd–Pd bonds gradually appeared. These data clearly suggest that the oxidation of Pd species was suppressed even upon exposure to NO, with the other metals acting as sacrificial species to prevent this oxidation. After switching to a H2 flow, the XANES spectrum regained the flat shape characteristic of the HEA. The FT-EXAFS spectrum also recovered the original HEA structure with decreasing and increasing intensity of peaks associated with long Pd–Pd bonds and short Pd–M bonds, respectively.

Based on the above discussion, the origin of the improved ORR performance of the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst can be explained as follows. First, compared with pure Pt, the high-entropy structure with a Pt-rich surface not only adjusts the adsorption energies of *O and *OH on the Pt/HEA and N–Pt/HEA surfaces, which support an enhanced electron transfer efficiency for the ORR, but also reduces OH poisoning, resulting directly in the high ORR activity of the HEA catalysts. Second, the N-doping could further regulate the binding strength during the intermediate transformation and consequently contribute to boosting the ORR activity and stability of the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst.
